data.title: Interview script (Probe B) — validating context loss between agent sessions
body: # Interview script (Probe B) — validating context loss between agent sessions
- **Date:** 2026-09-08 (rewritten from the script of 2026-09-02)
- **Type:** problem discovery (not solution validation)
- **Duration:** 45 minutes
- **Interviewees:** 5–7 developers in teams from 3 people up who **work with an AI coding agent every day**
- **Method:** Portigal (rapport, "tell me about the last time") + Fitzpatrick (*The Mom Test*) + Torres (stories instead of opinions)
## Why the script was rewritten

The previous version tested **merge conflicts and velocity**. The positioning changed on 2026-09-04 to **shared context**, and [Probe A](DOC-55) measured conflicts as real but rare — one merge in two hundred. The script was left as an instrument of the previous strategy.

The [discovery of 2026-09-08](DOC-44) shifted the question once more. The pain is described from outside — practitioners arrived at the format "decision, reason, rejected" on their own and named the mechanism. So asking "does the problem exist" is no longer worth doing: what is worth asking is **where they work around it today and what they are missing in that**.
## The three questions everything is for
1. **When did an agent last do the wrong thing because it did not know what the team knew — and what did the person do next?**
2. **Where does "why we did it this way" live right now — and what is wrong with that?**
3. Do conflicts and velocity come up at all on their own, without a prompt?
The third question is deliberately last. If they are not mentioned, that is an answer about the previous strategy, and it is needed too.
**kadence is not mentioned once.** Nor is any memory tool, MCP or ADR mentioned **first**. The moment I name the category, the interviewee answers about it rather than about their own work.
## Phase 1 — Opening (5 min)

> Thanks for agreeing to this. I'm researching how development teams work with AI agents — I'm not selling anything and I won't be showing you anything. What I'm interested in is how things actually work for you, including what works badly. There are no right answers here.
> Do you mind if I record this for my own notes? The recording won't go anywhere.
## Phase 2 — Context (7 min)
- Tell me what you're working on at the moment and what your team looks like.
- Which agent do you use, and for how long now? How many people on the team use it too?
- What do you track your tasks in? How did you end up on that one?
- *(if they moved from something else)* What happened that made you switch tools? ← **still the most valuable question in the interview**
## Phase 3 — Stories (23 min, the main part)
### Branch 1 — context loss between sessions *(the main one)*
- How do you usually start a new session with the agent on a task you'd already started earlier?
- **Tell me about the last time the agent suggested something you'd already tried and rejected.** What exactly did it suggest?
- How would it have known that this had been rejected?
- What did you do next — explain it again, roll it back, drop it?
- How long did that take?
- **Tell me about the last time you explained the same thing to the agent twice.**
- How often does that happen — daily, weekly, less often?
- Do you do anything to avoid it? *(stay silent and wait)*

The last question is the most important one in the script. **A workaround is evidence of pain, stronger than a complaint.** If a person does something about it, they are spending effort on it, and effort does not lie.
### Branch 2 — where the "why" lives
- When the team makes a decision — "we take X, we don't take Y" — where does that end up?
- **Tell me about the last time you had to work out why something was done a particular way.** Where did you look? Did you find it?
- Who on the team knows the most that isn't written down anywhere?
- *(if they do write something down)* Who reads it? When did anyone last look in there?
- Have you ever tried to fix this somehow? **What exactly did you try, and how did it end?**

- *(only after the stories, do not name kadence)* **When did an agent last do something wrong that wouldn't have happened if it had read your document?** Which document, where does it live, and why didn't the agent read it? *(P1 from [repo-docs-hypothesis](DOC-59): only a dated story with a named document counts)*

The last question opens the category of workarounds **without naming a single one**. If the interviewee says "ADR", "memory", "a rules file", "a compaction prompt" themselves — that is the most valuable data in the interview. If they do not say it, do not prompt.
### Branch 3 — conflicts and velocity *(secondary)*
Ask only if there is time left **or** if the interviewee brought them up themselves.
- How does merging a branch with tasks go for you? When did it last go wrong?
- How do you tell at the end of a sprint whether you got through it? Has anyone asked you for numbers?
## Phase 4 — Looking for contradictions (7 min)
Here I deliberately test what was said for strength.
- You said that re-telling the context is annoying — how many times has that happened this week? *(compare with what they said in Phase 3)*
- If tomorrow the agent remembered everything the team knows, what would change about your Tuesday?
- What annoys you most about working with the agent? *(if it is not context — that is the main result of the interview)*
- Are you paying for or installing anything for this right now? *(money and installation are the hardest signal)*
## Phase 5 — Closing (3 min)
- What should I have asked you that I didn't?
- Who else is worth asking about this?
## What not to ask
| Bad question | Why | Instead of it |
| "Would it be useful to you if the agent remembered decisions?" | hypothetical, a polite answer is guaranteed | "Tell me about the last time it didn't remember" |
| "Do you use ADRs / mem0 / MCP?" | names the category first, sets up the answer | "What have you tried to fix this?" |
| "How much would you pay for something like that?" | a worthless answer before the product exists | "Are you paying for anything for this right now?" |
| "Do you like the idea of a journal in the repository?" | a compliment instead of data | do not ask it at all |
## How to count the result
Within 30 minutes after each interview, record:
- **Story:** was there a concrete case of context loss **in the last 90 days** — yes/no. Further back than 90 days is reconstruction, not recollection
- **Consequence:** what the person actually did next and how long it took
- **Workaround:** what they already do to avoid it, and what they are missing in that
- **Where the "why" lives:** the place named, and whether anyone actually looks there
- **Contradiction:** where the words diverged from the behaviour
- **Surprise:** what I did not expect to hear
**Thresholds set in advance:**
| Result | Threshold |
| **Pain confirmed** | 4+ out of 7 give a concrete case **with a consequence** in the last 90 days |
| **A workaround exists** | 3+ describe an action they take precisely for this — a file, a prompt, a ritual, a tool |
| **Refutation** | "Yes, it's annoying" without a single story. Counts as a refutation, not as a confirmation |
| **Pivot** | 4+ name something else entirely as the main pain |

The second metric decides the fate of `kadence decision`: if there is no workaround, we are offering discipline rather than a tool — and disciplines, by the observation from the discovery, die from the absence of an operating model.
## The most likely result, and one to be ready for

The most expected: context loss will be confirmed readily — it is on everyone's lips right now — but the workarounds will turn out to be cheaper than our product. A rules file, a better prompt, a paid memory layer.

If so, the answer is not "the product is not needed" but **"it is needed, but not as a task tracker"** — and then the question is whether a journal of work should be the same instrument as an agent's memory at all.
This is the worst possible result for the current roadmap and the most useful one for the product.
